extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, critics, and informed readers interested in drama and stage morality
extracted.subtask_short: writing virtuous comedy for the stage
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and prescriptive standards for composing stage comedies that entertain while upholding moral taste and social good; compares English practice with ancient Greek and Roman theatrical norms. Focus is on what subjects, character-portrayals, and tone are appropriate for comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage virtue and moral influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage ought to be virtuous and to recommend religion, government, and public worship; if the English stage were as virtuous as the Greek or Roman, it would improve the behaviour of polite society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plays should contribute to the advancement of morality and the reformation of the age; they should not make it fashionable to ridicule religion or its professors. Example: Athenian plays recommended religion and public worship; the English stage should emulate that beneficial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation and inspection of plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should be subject to proper inspections and limitations so that theatrical entertainments refine rather than corrupt human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plays were regulated like ancient Athenian theatre, audiences would be edified and leave wiser and better than they came. Implies institutional or censorial oversight to restrain licentiousness and abusive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark and brand vices so they are not laudable
rubrics_metrics.description: When vices appear on the stage, the poet must ensure they are clearly marked as blameworthy and do not appear laudable or amiable in the person who is tainted with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation of vice should make the character appear censurable rather than attractive; avoid staging vices in ways that elicit sympathy or admiration for the wrongdoer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid choosing improper subjects for ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Never select subjects for ridicule that are apt to excite horror and commiseration rather than laughter; some topics are improper for comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper subjects: incest, murder, and violations of the marriage-bed — such matters gave rise to noble tragedies in antiquity and are unsuitable bases for comedy (Terence avoided these). Anti-pattern: building comedy around shocking or tragic acts that provoke pity rather than mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base comedy on cuckoldry and sexual degradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuckoldom and sexual humiliation should not be the recurrent basis of modern plays; making Aldermen, husbands, knights, baronets, country squires etc. appear primarily to be cuckolded is a corrupt practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the stock device where the 'accomplished gentleman' is portrayed as a whore‑master and the 'fine woman' as a jilt. This is an anti-pattern that degrades characters and audience taste; writers should invent finer models of character not predicated on sexual vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make criminals or immoral characters the favourites of the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets must avoid contrivances that cause the audience to root for the criminal or immoral characters throughout the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern described: dramatists contrive matters so that the two criminal lovers become audience favourites, eliciting wishes for their success. Instead, the dramatist should ensure that vice is unappealing and that virtuous characters retain audience sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish merry from lewd — avoid mere lewdness
rubrics_metrics.description: Low genius writers often confuse being merry with being lewd; comedy should be merry without descending into lewdness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productions should aim for wit, humour, and good sense rather than loose, unguarded strokes that pander to corrupt tastes. Keep clear moral and tasteful boundaries in jokes and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper subject-matter that stirs horror rather than laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Reiteration of the prohibition against treating grave crimes or morally shocking material as comedic fodder because those subjects provoke horror and commiseration, not laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the example that a Scipio or a Lelius would not regard incest or murder as fit for comedy; choose subjects that naturally invite laughter without ethical transgression or emotional distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and substance over frothy wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural writing is that which is pleasing and easy — a new thought or conceit expressed in smooth language — whereas mere frothy amusements (speculative, ornamented talk) are shallow and fit only for 'boys or silly women.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor sound judgment and profitable observation over the display of speculative wit; aim for ideas and expressions that are genuinely pleasing rather than merely ornate or artificially neat. Anti-pattern: writing that sacrifices substance for quaint language and contrived conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the stage to refine manners and discourage ridicule of respectable institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatre should not be a place to ridicule respectable institutions (religion, government) or to make the man of pleasure the model of a gentleman; rather it should uphold qualities ornamental to human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage portrayals that bring vanity and vice into discredit and give due esteem to virtues that ornament human nature. Example: If the stage followed ancient rules, vanity would be out of countenance and polite qualities would be esteemed.
